---
title: "Create Dataset with Effect Sizes of Ecosystem-Level Metrics"
output: html_document
date: "2022-11-15"
editor_options: 
  chunk_output_type: console

To analyse how strong the effects of the connection on the biomass, biodiversity, and population densities within ecosystems were, we want to compile a dataset (`ds_ecosystems_effect_size`) where each row represents the effect size of a connected vs unconnected ecosystem type (e.g., small autotrophic connected vs unconnected) at a time point. If the 95% CI of the effect size crosses the zero line it means that it is statistically significant. We use the effect size Hedge's d (aka Hedge's g), as it can handle the treatment and/or control equal to zero (log response ratio cannot: ln(treatment/0) = Inf; ln(0/control) = -inf; ln(0/0) = Nan), small sample sizes ("*it works well when there are as few as five to ten studies",* @Rosenberg2013), and unequal variance between treatment and control ([@Rosenberg2013]). Hedge's d (d) is the difference in mean between treatment and control divided by by their weighted spread (denominator) multiplied by a factor (J) that controls for small sample sizes [@Rosenberg2013]. The 95% confidence interval of Hedge's d is calculated from its standard error (SE) as [@Hedges1985] $d ± 1.96 * SE$ where the standard error is calculated as show in @Borenstein2009.

We calculate Hedge's d and its 95 % confidence interval in three steps. (1) Calculate means, standard deviations and sample sizes. Calculate the mean of the treatment (Y1) and control (Y2), the standard deviation of the treatment (s1) and the control (s2), as well as the sample size of the treatment (n1) and the control (n2) at each time point and for each response variable. (2) Calculate Hedge's d. Use means, standard deviations and sample sizes to calculate effect sizes. (3) Retain only the treatments (connected ecosystems), discarding the controls (unconnected). This is because we calculated the effect size of only connected compared to unconnected and not the other way around.

$$
d = \frac{Y1 - Y2}{denominator} * J
$$

$$
denominator = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)*s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1) * s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}
$$

$$
J = 1 - \frac{3}{(4 * (n_1 + n_2 - 2)) - 1}
$$

$$
SE = \sqrt{J^2 * \frac{n_1 + n_2}{n_1*n_2} + \frac{d^2}{2*(n_1 + n_2)}}
$$

<br>

```{r calculate-means-sd-and-sample-sizes}

# --- CALCULATE MEANS, STANDARD DEVIATIONS, AND SAMPLE SIZES FOR EACH ECOSYSTEM VARIABLE --- #
# We'll use these information to calculate effect sizes

## Loop through each variable in the 'variables_ecosystems' vector to calculate 
# means, standard deviations, and sample sizes for each ecosystem variable.

for (i in 1:length(variables_ecosystems)) {
  
  # Create a new dataset for each ecosystem variable
  
  ds_ecosystems_effect_size[[i]] = ds_ecosystems %>%
    
    # Filter out rows where the current ecosystem variable is NA.
    
    filter(!is.na(!!sym(variables_ecosystems[i]))) %>%
    
    # For each treatment at each time point calculate the mean , 
    #standard deviation, and sample size of the current variable
    
    group_by(across(all_of(c("time_point",
                             "day",
                             "ecosystem_size_ml",
                             "trophic_type",
                             "connection",
                             "disturbance_percentage")))) %>%
    summarise(across(all_of(variables_ecosystems[i]),
                     list(mean = mean,   
                          sd = sd)),     
              sample_size = n()) %>%
    
    # Rename the sample size column to include the variable name 
    # for clarity in future operations.
    
    rename_with( ~ paste0(variables_ecosystems[i], 
                          "_sample_size"),
                 matches("sample_size"))
}

# After processing each variable, combine the results into a single dataset.
# The full_join() function merges the datasets by the key grouping columns,
# so that each treatment has its means, standard deviations, and sample sizes 
# in separate columns.

ds_ecosystems_effect_size <- reduce(ds_ecosystems_effect_size,
                                    full_join,
                                    by = c("time_point",
                                           "day",
                                           "ecosystem_size_ml",
                                           "trophic_type",
                                           "connection",
                                           "disturbance_percentage"))
```

```{r calculate-effect-sizes-using-Hedges-d}

# --- CALCULATE EFFECT SIZE USING THE METRIC HEDGE'S D --- #

# Initialize the effect size columns (Hedge's d and its confidence intervals for each variable)

for (i in length(variables_ecosystems)) {
  ds_ecosystems_effect_size <- ds_ecosystems_effect_size %>%
    mutate(!!paste0(variables_ecosystems[i], "_d") := NA,          # Column for Hedge's d
           !!paste0(variables_ecosystems[i], "_d_upper") := NA,    # Column for upper CI of d
           !!paste0(variables_ecosystems[i], "_d_lower") := NA)    # Column for lower CI of d
}

# Add a new column 'ecosystem_type' that combines multiple variables (ecosystem size, 
# trophic type, disturbance percentage) to define the ecosystem's identity.

ds_ecosystems_effect_size = ds_ecosystems_effect_size %>%
  mutate(ecosystem_type = paste(ecosystem_size_ml, "ml", trophic_type, disturbance_percentage))

# Initialize a row counter to track the iteration number

row_n = 0  

# Store the unique ecosystem types in 'ecosystem_treatments'

ecosystem_treatments = unique(ds_ecosystems_effect_size$ecosystem_type)

# For each treatment, time point, and variable calculate Hedge's d and 95% CI

for (treatment_i in 1:length(ecosystem_treatments)) {

  for (time_point_i in 0:(length(time_points)-1)) {

    row_n = row_n + 1  # Increment the row counter for each iteration
    
    # Filter the data for the current treatment (connected ecosystems)
    
    treatment_row = ds_ecosystems_effect_size %>%
      filter(ecosystem_type == ecosystem_treatments[treatment_i],
             connection == "connected",               
             time_point == time_points[time_point_i+1]) 

    # Filter the data for the current control (unconnected ecosystems)
    
    control_row = ds_ecosystems_effect_size %>%
      filter(ecosystem_type == ecosystem_treatments[treatment_i],
             connection == "unconnected",             
             time_point == time_points[time_point_i+1]) 

    # Loop through each variable in the ecosystem data (variables_ecosystems)
    
    for (variable_i in 1:length(variables_ecosystems)) {

      # Calculate Hedge's d effect size
      # This requires mean, standard deviation, and sample size for both 
      # treatment and control groups
      
      hedges_d = calculate.hedges_d(
        treatment_row[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_mean")]],  # Mean of treatment group
        treatment_row[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_sd")]],    # SD of treatment group
        treatment_row[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_sample_size")]], # Sample size of treatment group
        control_row[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_mean")]],    # Mean of control group
        control_row[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_sd")]],      # SD of control group
        control_row[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_sample_size")]])  # Sample size of control group

      # Store the calculated Hedge's d effect size in the appropriate column
      
      ds_ecosystems_effect_size[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_d")]][
        ds_ecosystems_effect_size$ecosystem_type == ecosystem_treatments[treatment_i] &
        ds_ecosystems_effect_size$time_point == time_points[time_point_i+1]] =
        hedges_d$d  # Store Hedge's d

      # Store the upper confidence interval of Hedge's d in the appropriate 
      # column
      
      ds_ecosystems_effect_size[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_d_upper")]][
        ds_ecosystems_effect_size$ecosystem_type == ecosystem_treatments[treatment_i] &
        ds_ecosystems_effect_size$time_point == time_points[time_point_i+1]] =
        hedges_d$upper_CI  # Store upper CI

      # Store the lower confidence interval of Hedge's d in the appropriate 
      # column
      
      ds_ecosystems_effect_size[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_d_lower")]][
        ds_ecosystems_effect_size$ecosystem_type == ecosystem_treatments[treatment_i] &
        ds_ecosystems_effect_size$time_point == time_points[time_point_i+1]] =
        hedges_d$lower_CI  # Store lower CI
    }
  }
}

# Retain only the connected ecosystems

ds_ecosystems_effect_size = ds_ecosystems_effect_size %>%
  filter(connection == "connected")
```

However, Hedge's d because of how much it depends on the pooled spread of the treatment and control might be harder to interpret than the log response ratio. Therefore, even though the log response ratio might not be calculated for all the protist species, we also decide to calculate it as well. To calculate the log response ratio of the dominance of protist species I use here the package `SingleCaseES` (see [this link](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/SingleCaseES/vignettes/Using-SingleCaseES.html)). This package. The package provides the function `LRRi` which calculates effect sizes for a single study case. It also adjust for small sample sizes by default.

```{r calculate-effect-sizes-using-LRR}

# --- CACLCULATE THE EFFECT SIZE USING THE METRIC LRR --- #

# Initialise the effect size columns 

for (variable_i in length(variables_ecosystems)) {
  ds_ecosystems_effect_size <- ds_ecosystems_effect_size %>%
    mutate(!!paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_LRR") := NA,
           !!paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_LRR_upper") := NA,
           !!paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_LRR_lower") := NA)
}
  
row_n = 0

# For each treatment, time point, and variable calculate LRR and 95% CI

for (treatment_i in 1:length(ecosystem_treatments)) {
    
  for (time_point_i in 0:(length(time_points)-1)) {
    
      for (variable_i in 1:length(variables_ecosystems)) {
        
        row_n = row_n + 1
        
        # Filter the data for the current treatment (connected ecosystems)
        
        treatment_values = ds_ecosystems %>%
          mutate(ecosystem_type = paste(ecosystem_size_ml, "ml", trophic_type, disturbance_percentage)) %>%
          filter(ecosystem_type == ecosystem_treatments[treatment_i],
                 connection == "connected",
                 time_point == time_points[time_point_i+1],
                 !is.na(!!sym(variables_ecosystems[variable_i]))) %>%
          pull(!!sym(variables_ecosystems[variable_i]))
        
        # Filter the data for the current control (unconnected ecosystems)
        
        control_values = ds_ecosystems %>%
          mutate(ecosystem_type = paste(ecosystem_size_ml, "ml", trophic_type, disturbance_percentage)) %>%
          filter(ecosystem_type == ecosystem_treatments[treatment_i],
                 connection == "unconnected",
                 time_point == time_points[time_point_i+1],
                 !is.na(!!sym(variables_ecosystems[variable_i]))) %>%
          pull(!!sym(variables_ecosystems[variable_i]))
    
        # By default it corrects for small sample sizes and calculates 95 % CI.
        
        LRR_output = LRRi(A_data = control_values, 
                          B_data = treatment_values, 
                          scale = "proportion")
        
        # Store the calculated LRR effect size in the appropriate column
        
        ds_ecosystems_effect_size[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_LRR")]][
          ds_ecosystems_effect_size$ecosystem_type ==
           ecosystem_treatments[treatment_i] &
          ds_ecosystems_effect_size$time_point == 
           time_points[time_point_i+1]] =
          LRR_output$Est
        
        # Store the upper confidence interval of LRR in the appropriate 
        # column
        
        ds_ecosystems_effect_size[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_LRR_upper")]][
          ds_ecosystems_effect_size$ecosystem_type ==
           ecosystem_treatments[treatment_i] &
          ds_ecosystems_effect_size$time_point == 
           time_points[time_point_i+1]] =
          LRR_output$CI_upper
        
        # Store the lower confidence interval of LRR in the appropriate 
        # column
        
        ds_ecosystems_effect_size[[paste0(variables_ecosystems[variable_i], "_LRR_lower")]][
          ds_ecosystems_effect_size$ecosystem_type ==
           ecosystem_treatments[treatment_i] &
          ds_ecosystems_effect_size$time_point == 
           time_points[time_point_i+1]] =
          LRR_output$CI_lower
        
      }
    }
  }
```
